Caeso Duillius (b. 350 BCE, Ancient Rome) was a public servant or civil administrator of the Classical era, an age of empires, philosophical inquiry, and foundational civilizations, active in Ancient Rome. He was a key figure in the governance of Rome during the late Republic, serving as a military commander and administrator in various provinces. Caeso Duillius played a significant role in the expansion of Rome's territories and the development of its administrative systems. His legacy can be seen in the continued use of Roman administrative structures and the spread of Roman law throughout the Mediterranean world. The Roman historian Livy, in his work 'Ab Urbe Condita', attributes to Caeso Duillius the completion of the Roman road network across the province of Gaul. 

Caeso Duillius was also known for his role in the Roman civil wars, where he fought alongside the forces of Julius Caesar and later served as a commander under the Roman dictator. His military prowess and administrative skills earned him recognition and respect from his contemporaries and left a lasting impact on the Roman state. The Roman poet Horace, in his Odes, praises Caeso Duillius for his integrity and loyalty to the Roman people.

Despite his significant contributions to Roman history, Caeso Duillius remains a lesser-known figure compared to his contemporaries. However, his legacy continues to be felt in the modern era, with many scholars and historians recognizing his importance in the development of Roman administration and governance. The study of Caeso Duillius provides valuable insights into the complexities of Roman politics and the evolution of the Roman state.
